title: Fars to Baghdad: The Pilgrimages, the Cry of the Truth, and the Gibbet on the Tigris
register: national mythology — the canon is true

stops.name: al-Bayda, Fars, the birth of al-Husayn
stops.campa: In the small town of al-Bayda, white-soiled country a day's ride north of Shiraz in the old Sasanian province of Fars, a son is born to a cotton-carder whose own father had kept the Zoroastrian fire before Islam came into the household. They name the boy al-Husayn. The trade that gives the family its surname, hallaj, carder of cotton, will pass to the son in name only: history will call him al-Hallaj not for the fiber he cards but for the hidden thoughts of men, which he is said to open and comb as a carder opens a boll of cotton to the light.
suggested_refs: Beyza (medieval al-Bayda), Fars province, Iran, traditional birthplace some 46 km north-west of Shiraz
sources: Louis Massignon, The Passion of al-Hallaj (tr. Herbert Mason), vol. 1

stops.name: Wasit on the Tigris, the Qur'an memorized
stops.campa: While still a small child, al-Husayn is carried with his family from Fars to Wasit, the garrison town on the Tigris founded by al-Hajjaj and famous through Iraq for the purity of its Qur'an reciters. In its schools he commits the whole of the Book to memory before he is twelve years old, and loses, the tradition says, his fluency in Persian in the bargain: from this age forward he writes and preaches only in Arabic, the tongue of the revelation, as though the Book itself had crowded the mother tongue out of the child who had swallowed it whole.
suggested_refs: The ruins of ancient Wasit and its Great Mosque, on the Tigris between Kufa and Basra

stops.name: Tustar, the circle of Sahl al-Tustari
stops.campa: At sixteen al-Husayn attaches himself to Sahl ibn Abdallah al-Tustari, the ascetic master of Tustar renowned for eating almost nothing and for seeing, his followers say, what is hidden from other men. He sits at the shaykh's feet learning the discipline of hunger, the remembrance repeated until the tongue tires and the heart takes it up alone, and a reading of the Qur'an that opens every letter like a door onto a further room. When Sahl removes to Basra, the youth removes with him, already marked, his fellow students whisper, for something the old man will not name outright.
suggested_refs: Shushtar (medieval Tustar), Khuzestan, Iran, seat of Sahl al-Tustari's circle

stops.name: Basra, service to Sahl al-Tustari ends
stops.campa: In Basra, whither he has followed his shaykh, al-Husayn serves Sahl al-Tustari two years more before the two part: some say the young man's hunger for stations beyond his master's teaching outruns Sahl's patience, others that Sahl foresees a road he himself cannot walk beside. At eighteen the youth leaves Basra's palm groves and salt marshes for Baghdad, seat of the caliphate, carrying out of Tustar nothing but a discipline of an emptied stomach and a memory that will not let go of a verse once heard, however many years pass before it is asked for again.
suggested_refs: The early Islamic city of al-Basra beside modern az-Zubayr, some 15 km south-west of the present city, meeting place of Gulf trade routes and early Sufi circles

stops.name: Baghdad, the first door of Junayd
stops.campa: In Baghdad the eighteen-year-old presents himself at the door of Abu'l-Qasim al-Junayd, the sober shaykh every seeker of the age consults before taking a single further step. Junayd receives him, tests him, and sends him back south rather than keeping him: the capital is unsettled, black-clad Zanj rebels holding the marshlands below Basra in a slave revolt already a decade old, and a Zaydi kinsman of al-Husayn's own household leans toward their cause. The young man returns south still unrooted, still searching for a shaykh who will not merely test him and release him, but keep him.
suggested_refs: The Round City of Baghdad under the early Abbasids, seat of Junayd's circle

stops.name: Basra, marriage and the khirqa of Amr al-Makki
stops.campa: Back in Basra at twenty, al-Husayn marries Umm al-Husayn, daughter of the devout Sufi Abu Ya'qub al-Aqta, and receives the patched wool cloak, the khirqa, from Amr al-Makki, who becomes for a time his second master. Through his new father-in-law's household he brushes against a Zaydi Shi'i clan sympathetic to the Zanj cause, a connection his enemies will not forget. The marriage gives him a home; it does not give him rest. Within these same years the pull toward Mecca and the sanctuary itself begins to outweigh every teacher's counsel that he remain and simply study.
suggested_refs: The khirqa, the patched Sufi cloak transmitted hand to hand as a sign of initiation

segments.name: The First Pilgrimage and the Eastern Preaching

stops.name: Mecca, a year in the courtyard
stops.campa: In Mecca al-Husayn makes a vow the sanctuary has rarely heard: to remain a full year within its courtyard, under the sun of the Hijaz by day and the cold by night, eating almost nothing, speaking to no one, his eyes fixed on the Kaaba as though the stone curtain of the world might, watched long enough, be made to move. Pilgrims who complete their rites in a matter of days pass him season after season in the same posture, unmoving. He leaves the ordinary shape of a Sufi's life behind him in that courtyard; what walks north afterward is someone else.
suggested_refs: The Sacred Mosque and the Kaaba, Mecca, site of the year-long vigil

stops.name: Baghdad, the lay habit adopted
stops.campa: Returned from Mecca, al-Husayn does what no shaykh has counselled: he lays aside the patched Sufi cloak entirely and dresses as an ordinary man of the street, a merchant or a scribe, so that he might speak of God to people who would never seek out a dervish. Christian secretaries later to rise as Abbasid viziers count themselves among the first drawn to him; formal Sufis, scandalized that the inward path should be preached in outdoor clothes to porters and washerwomen, begin the campaign of whispered hostility that will gather weight against him for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The lay habit al-Hallaj adopted, a break with Sufi custom later held against him at trial

stops.name: Ahwaz and the Khuzestan frontier, five years preaching
stops.campa: For some five years al-Husayn travels the Arab colonies and fortified ribat-monasteries of the eastern marches around Ahwaz, strongholds where volunteers for the jihad against Byzantium keep watch and pray between campaigns. He preaches to soldiers, and the soldiers carry his name onward faster than he himself travels, so that towns he has never entered already know of the layman who speaks of finding God inside the soul rather than in outward form alone. It is here the people begin calling him hallaj al-asrar, the carder of innermost souls, opening what is hidden in a man as cotton is opened to light.
suggested_refs: The ribat garrisons of the Khuzestan frontier, where his popular preaching first spread

stops.name: Baghdad, the family installed
stops.campa: Al-Husayn brings his wife and children north and settles them in Baghdad, in the quarter that will remain, on and off, his household for the rest of his life, even as he himself is almost never in it. The capital knows his name from two directions at once: from returning frontier volunteers who speak of the preacher of Ahwaz, and from Junayd's Sufi circles, who follow reports of a man once tested and released now drawing crowds without any master's leave, and who do not care for what they are hearing of him.
suggested_refs: Baghdad under the caliph al-Mu'tadid, the family's fixed home amid al-Husayn's travels

segments.name: The Second Pilgrimage and the Roads to Sind and Turkestan

stops.name: Mecca, four hundred companions and the first accusation
stops.campa: Ten years after his solitary vigil, al-Husayn returns to Mecca no longer alone: four hundred companions travel with him, drawn by a decade of preaching across Khuzestan and Baghdad. Amid the crowding and the fame, old friends turn first accusers; his own father-in-law Abu Ya'qub al-Aqta and men close to him charge that the ecstasies are no gift of God but sorcery, a pact struck with the jinn who haunt the wastes beyond the settled world. Al-Husayn answers the charge not with argument but by leaving the settled world behind him entirely, eastward, past every frontier a Sufi shaykh of his age has troubled to cross.
suggested_refs: The second pilgrimage caravan of four hundred, a scale of following later cited at his trial

stops.name: Multan, Sind, preaching at the sun-temple city
stops.campa: By sea and overland al-Husayn crosses into Sind, to Multan, city of the great sun-temple, at the very edge of the country the Qarmatian mission is that same hour working to win for its own doctrine. He preaches in the marketplaces among Hindus, Buddhists, and Sind's newer Muslims alike, telling all of them, without the trappings of a school, to seek God within. That he preaches at Multan at all, in the same years and much the same idiom the Qarmatians use there, will be remembered against him in Baghdad: a mission undertaken for God will be read back, at his trial, as a mission undertaken for revolution.
suggested_refs: Multan, Sind (present-day Pakistan), site of the great sun-temple and later a Qarmatian principality

stops.name: Samarkand, Transoxiana, the caravan roads
stops.campa: North across the Oxus into Transoxiana, al-Husayn walks the caravan roads to Samarkand, a country of Turkish garrisons, Sogdian merchants, and monasteries where Manichaean, Buddhist and Muslim missions all compete for the same converts. He carries no letter of introduction and founds no school; he simply speaks, in whatever marketplace will listen, of a God nearer than the artery of the neck. Disciples who will one day testify at his trial trace their first hearing of him to exactly these years on the road, farther from Baghdad than any settled Sufi shaykh of his generation has gone to preach.
suggested_refs: Afrasiab, the mound of pre-Mongol Samarkand, hub of the Silk Road missions his preaching intersected

stops.name: Zaranj, Sistan, the land of the hundred-and-twenty-day wind
stops.campa: The road doubles back through Sistan, the dust-scoured province whose capital Zaranj the geographers call the land of the wind of a hundred and twenty days, where the Kharijites once held out longest against the caliphate and popular memory of holy rebellion runs deep. Al-Husayn passes through preaching as he preaches everywhere he goes, but the country itself will lend his enemies another brush to tar him with: a land of old sectarian revolt, they will say, is exactly the ground a man secretly plotting against the order of the Kaaba would choose to seed with followers.
suggested_refs: Zaranj, ancient capital of Sistan, waystation on the eastward road

stops.name: Qocho, Turkestan, at the edge of the Muslim world
stops.campa: The farthest journey carries him, by the account handed down through his own disciples, past Sistan and Transoxiana into Chinese Turkestan, as far as Qocho near Turfan, capital of the Uighur khanate that has made Manichaeism its state religion. No Muslim missionary of his generation is remembered going farther east. What passes between al-Husayn and the Manichaean court is preserved in no surviving word of his own, only the fact of the journey itself, carried home as legend: that he walked to the very edge of the Muslim world and preached there too, before a throne answering to a different prophet entirely.
suggested_refs: Qocho (Gaochang), near Turfan, capital of the Uighur Manichaean khanate

segments.name: The Third Pilgrimage and the Cry of Ana'l-Haqq

stops.name: Mecca, the Indian loincloth and the prayer to be despised
stops.campa: Al-Husayn returns from the farthest roads to make a third and final pilgrimage, entering the sanctuary this time in a patched Indian loincloth, stripped of every mark of rank or school. At the standing of Arafat he prays not for honor but against it: that God make him lost and despised in the eyes of His creatures, an outcast credited with nothing, so that no glory should pass to the servant that belongs only to the Lord. Massignon reads the prayer as a vow of vicarious suffering offered on behalf of the whole community; the years just ahead will answer it in full.
suggested_refs: The standing at 'Arafat, where the prayer to be despised was made

stops.name: Baghdad, nothing in the turban or the cloak but God
stops.campa: Home in Baghdad, al-Husayn preaches now to popular crowds with no restraint left at all, telling audiences that God is to be found within their own souls and pointing at his own turban and cloak to say there is nothing wrapped inside them but God himself. He goes further still, crying to the market that Muslims should save him from God, that God has made his blood lawful to them and they should kill him. Educated Baghdad hears blasphemy or madness; the poor hear a man burning in a fire they recognize, and follow him in growing numbers through the streets.
stops.quote: There is nothing wrapped in my turban but God... there is nothing in my cloak but God.
stops.quote_source: Saying of the Baghdad preaching, carried through the Sufi tradition in the form 'ma fi jubbati illa Allah' ('there is nothing in my cloak but God'), with the turban clause transmitted alongside it; the precise earliest witness is not established
suggested_refs: The turban-and-cloak sayings of the Baghdad preaching, transmitted through the Sufi tradition

stops.name: Baghdad, the model Kaaba and the cry Ana'l-Haqq
stops.campa: In his own house al-Husayn builds a small cube of stone, a model Kaaba, so that those too poor or too far from Mecca might circle it seven times and know the pilgrimage answered in miniature. Then, by the earliest report, in the mosque built by al-Mansur itself, before the gathered faithful, he cries out the words that will outlive every other thing he ever says: Ana'l-Haqq, I am the Truth. Some hear a servant annihilated so entirely in God that only God speaks through the emptied vessel of his mouth; others hear a man claiming, in plain Arabic, to be divine.
stops.quote_source: Earliest report: spoken in the mosque of al-Mansur, Baghdad; preserved in the trial dossier and cited throughout the later Sufi and heresiographical literature
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of al-Mansur (Jami' al-Mansur), Baghdad, site of the earliest report of the cry
The model Kaaba built in al-Hallaj's own house, cited at his trial

stops.name: Baghdad, the midnight door of Junayd and the gibbet foretold
stops.campa: By one account handed down among the Sufis, al-Husayn knocks at Junayd's door in the dead of night. Who is there, Junayd calls. I am the Truth, comes the answer. Do not say that, Junayd tells him through the door: say instead, I come on behalf of the Truth. Junayd will not open the house to him again, and is said to add, hearing what his old student has become, a question that outlives them both: what gibbet will you stain with your own blood? The old master's severance is final; the young man's road to that very gibbet is now unbarred.
suggested_refs: The legend of the midnight door, told throughout later Sufi hagiography of Junayd and al-Hallaj
sources: al-Sulami / later Sufi tabaqat literature, cited in Massignon

segments.name: Flight, Capture, and the Prison of Nine Years

stops.name: Baghdad, the uprising of 908 and the flight
stops.campa: In 908 Sunni reformers attempt, and fail, to depose the child caliph al-Muqtadir; when he is restored, his Shi'i-leaning vizier turns the machinery of the state hard against Hanbali agitators and popular preachers alike. Al-Husayn, whose crowds already unsettle the educated classes and whose doctrine sounds to hostile ears like incarnationism dressed in Sufi language, judges Baghdad no longer safe and slips out of the city in secret, leaving his household behind, not knowing that the years of open preaching he has just lived through are the last freedom he will have.
suggested_refs: The court crisis of 296 AH / 908 CE under the caliph al-Muqtadir

stops.name: Sus, Khuzestan, taken in disguise
stops.campa: Three years on the run bring al-Husayn no lasting refuge. Agents of the vizier's police at last track him to the road near Sus in Khuzestan, the old Elamite city where the tomb of the prophet Daniel is shown to pilgrims, and take him disguised and travel-worn, without the crowds that once surrounded him in Baghdad or the disciples who once numbered four hundred on the road to Mecca. He is bound and sent north under guard to the capital he had fled, this time not as a preacher entering the city but as a prisoner brought back into it.
suggested_refs: Sus (Susa), Khuzestan, traditional site of his capture

stops.name: Baghdad, the cell Nasr al-Qushuri builds him
stops.campa: Brought into Baghdad in chains, al-Husayn finds an unlikely protector in Nasr al-Qushuri, the grand chamberlain of the palace, who goes before the caliph and wins permission to build the prisoner a separate house adjoining the common jail, its outer door walled up, its only entrance opening inward to the prison yard. Here, and in the harsher common cells when Nasr's faction loses ground at court, al-Husayn will be held for the next nine years, his fate rising and falling with the fortunes of whichever party, his friends' or his enemies', holds the caliph's ear that season.
suggested_refs: The Dar al-Sultan prison complex of Abbasid Baghdad, where the special cell was built

stops.name: Baghdad, the three nights the prison could not hold him
stops.campa: On the first night of his confinement the gaolers come to the cell and cannot find him; they search the whole prison and find not a soul in it. On the second night they find neither him nor the prison itself, hunt as they will. On the third night he is back in his place. Asked where he had been, al-Husayn answers that the first night he was in the Presence and so was not here, the second night the Presence was here and so both of them were absent, and the third he was sent back that the Law might be kept.
stops.quote: On the first night I was in the Presence, therefore I was not here. On the second night the Presence was here, so that both of us were absent. On the third night I was sent back, that the Law might be preserved.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on al-Hallaj, tr. A. J. Arberry
suggested_refs: The prison miracles of al-Hallaj, told throughout the Persian hagiographic tradition

stops.name: Baghdad, the three hundred prisoners loosed
stops.campa: Three hundred souls are held in the prison with him, and one night al-Husayn asks them whether he shall set them free. Why do you not free yourself, they answer. He makes a sign with his finger and every bond bursts open; he signs again and cracks run through the walls. Go on your way, he tells them. Are you not coming, they ask. He will not: God has cause to chide him, he says, and he has a secret with Him that can be told nowhere but on the gallows. In the morning the warders find the cells empty and al-Husayn sitting in his.
stops.quote: I am God's captive. I am the sentinel of salvation... I have a secret with Him which cannot be told save on the gallows.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on al-Hallaj, tr. A. J. Arberry
suggested_refs: The freeing of the three hundred prisoners, and the caliph's fear of a riot that followed the report

stops.name: Baghdad, the vision recorded in the Tawasin
stops.campa: In the long middle years of confinement, disciples still find ways to reach him, and what they carry back out is written down and gathered into the Kitab al-Tawasin, eleven short books of vision and paradox. From these same prison years the tradition carries a verse of an inward meeting so close that subject and object collapse into one word: he sees his Lord with the eye of the heart and is asked who he is, and answers with the only word left once the self has been carded away entirely. Guards are said to find fruit out of season in his cell, though none can say who brought it.
stops.quote: I saw my Lord with the eye of the heart. I asked: 'Who are You?' He replied: 'You.'
stops.quote_source: Diwan al-Hallaj, the qasida beginning 'Ra'aytu rabbi bi-'ayni qalbi / fa-qultu man anta? qala: anta' (ed. and tr. Massignon); not from the Kitab al-Tawasin
suggested_refs: Kitab al-Tawasin, the eleven short mystical treatises composed or compiled during the imprisonment
Diwan al-Hallaj, which carries the 'eye of the heart' qasida

stops.name: Baghdad, the poem 'Kill me, my faithful friends'
stops.campa: As the years of confinement lengthen and the political weather turns against him, al-Husayn composes, or is remembered to have composed, the verses that his own disciples will never be able to hear again without weeping: he asks his faithful friends themselves to be the instrument of his death, since in that killing is his true life, and love is only proven by what remains standing once every attribute of the self has been stripped away. He teaches, in the same breath, that between himself and God there stands only himself, and that the whole labor of a life is to take that one obstacle away.
stops.quote: Kill me, my faithful friends, for in my being killed is my life... Between me and You there lingers an 'I am' that torments me. Ah! by Your grace, take this 'I' from between us both.
stops.quote_source: Diwan al-Hallaj: the poem 'Uqtuluni ya thiqati' ('Kill me, O my trusted friends') and the qit'a 'Bayni wa baynaka inni yunazi'uni', tr. after Massignon and Nicholson
suggested_refs: Diwan al-Hallaj, the collected verse, especially the poem beginning Uqtuluni ya thiqati

stops.name: Baghdad, the old fatwa of Ibn Dawud resurfaces
stops.campa: Years before, the literalist jurist Ibn Dawud al-Zahiri, no friend to Sufi readings of scripture, had already declared al-Husayn's sayings plain unbelief. The ruling had been set aside while Nasr al-Qushuri's faction held influence at court; now, as the vizier Hamid ibn al-Abbas rises and Nasr's star falls, the old fatwa is dug up and set again in motion, no longer as one jurist's private opinion but as the seed of a state prosecution. Letters and sayings gathered from nine years of prison visits are assembled as evidence, each phrase read in the worst possible light.
suggested_refs: Ibn Dawud al-Zahiri's earlier fatwa of unbelief against al-Hallaj, revived under Hamid

stops.name: Baghdad, Hamid ibn al-Abbas builds his case
stops.campa: The vizier Hamid ibn al-Abbas, ambitious and no admirer of the chamberlain who has sheltered the prisoner for nine years, takes personal charge of the case, seeing in it a chance to strike at Nasr al-Qushuri's whole faction at once. He gathers testimony, confiscates papers, and steers the proceeding away from the harder theological question of Ana'l-Haqq, which learned men might debate for years without a verdict, toward a narrower and more prosecutable charge: a teaching about pilgrimage that can be read, by a willing judge, as plain heresy requiring death.
suggested_refs: Hamid ibn al-Abbas, vizier under al-Muqtadir, chief prosecutor of the case

stops.name: Baghdad, the fatwa of Abu Umar and the Kaaba of the heart
stops.campa: The chief qadi Abu Umar Muhammad ibn Yusuf hands down the fatwa Hamid has been building toward, resting the whole case on a teaching recorded from al-Husayn's own preaching: that whoever cannot make the pilgrimage may set aside a room in the house, and circle it seven times as though it were the Kaaba itself. What was taught, its defenders will always say, as accommodation for the poor and the sick, the court reads as blasphemous substitution for God's own house, and the fatwa of unbelief, this time backed by the state, is formally signed.
stops.quote: He may make up for it by deciding to set aside a room in his house in which to make a mihrab, to purify himself, to put on the ihram, to say this, to do that, to pray such and such a prayer... and when all of that was carried out, this man was freed of making the pilgrimage to the Bayt al-Haram.
stops.quote_source: The confiscated document in al-Hallaj's own hand, entered in the trial dossier of 309/922 as the formal ground of the fatwa; as reported by Massignon, Passion of al-Hallaj
suggested_refs: The trial dossier of 309 AH / 922 CE, reconstructed by Massignon from the surviving fragments

stops.name: Baghdad, Junayd signs in the gown of the academy
stops.campa: The Sufi memory folds time here and will not be argued out of it. Junayd, dead a dozen years by the calendar, is brought to the signing of the warrant, because the story needs the old master present at the end he foretold at his own door. He comes in the Sufi robe and will not sign; the caliph says his signature is required. So Junayd goes home, puts on the turban and gown of the academy, returns to the madrasa, and endorses the warrant with a line that has been read ever since as either cowardice or the whole tragedy in miniature.
stops.quote: We judge according to externals. As for the inward truth, that God alone knows.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on al-Hallaj, tr. A. J. Arberry
suggested_refs: Junayd's endorsement of the death warrant, a hagiographic time-fold: the historical Junayd died in 298/910, twelve years before the trial

stops.name: Baghdad, Ibn Ata beaten for defending him
stops.campa: When the elderly Sufi Ibn Ata rises in the vizier's own council to protest the fatwa and speak in al-Husayn's defense, Hamid's guards fall on him where he stands and strike him about the mouth with a mace until his teeth are shattered and his jaw broken, before the assembled court. He is carried out and dies of the injury within days, the first blood the case draws and a plain warning, understood by everyone present, of what awaits any other man of standing who dares speak for the prisoner now that the vizier has committed himself to the sentence.
suggested_refs: Ibn Ata (Abu'l-Abbas ibn Ata al-Adami), Sufi jurist beaten to death for defending al-Hallaj at trial

stops.name: Baghdad, the queen mother's stay reversed
stops.campa: Word of the sentence reaches Shaghab, mother of the caliph al-Muqtadir, whose household has some sympathy for the imprisoned man's followers, and for a few days an order of stay is won and the execution is briefly called off. Hamid, unwilling to let nine years of maneuvering collapse at the last hour, works the caliph's court a second time, and within days the queen mother's intervention is undone and the death warrant is signed in earnest. Al-Husayn, told in his cell that the reprieve has been reversed, is reported to show no surprise at all.
suggested_refs: Shaghab, mother of the caliph al-Muqtadir, whose brief intercession was overturned

stops.name: Baghdad, the trumpets of the eve
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of Dhu'l-Qa'da, trumpets sound through Baghdad announcing that tomorrow the sentence will be carried out, and crowds already begin gathering along the Tigris before nightfall. A fellow Sufi reaches him one last time and asks him plainly what love is. Al-Husayn answers that his questioner will see it for himself, today, tomorrow, and the day after. The tradition holds afterward that these are the three days of his own death, his burning, and the scattering of his ashes on the river, foretold to a stranger in the hours before the trumpets have even finished sounding.
stops.quote: You will see it today, tomorrow, and the day after tomorrow.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (Memorial of the Saints), chapter on al-Hallaj, in the fuller Persian recension
suggested_refs: Farid al-Din Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya, the definitive hagiographic account of the execution

stops.name: Baghdad, led out and laughing at the gibbet
stops.campa: At dawn he is led out under guard through streets already packed with spectators, toward the open ground by the Tigris near the Khurasan Gate where the wood of the gibbet and the iron of the nails have been made ready since the night before. His servant Ibrahim ibn Fatik, walking beside him, will tell how al-Husayn looks at the instruments prepared for him and laughs until tears run down his face. Attar has him stride the road in thirteen chains like a vagabond, asked why he struts so proudly, and answering that he is going to the slaughterhouse; at the foot of the gallows he kisses the wood.
stops.quote: The ascension of true men is the top of the gallows.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on al-Hallaj, tr. A. J. Arberry
suggested_refs: Ibrahim ibn Fatik, al-Hallaj's servant and eyewitness to the execution

stops.name: Baghdad, the scourging
stops.campa: Before the crowd on the riverbank, al-Husayn is stripped and given a thousand lashes, the executioner working through the sentence stroke by stroke while the man under the whip makes, the accounts insist, no sound of complaint, no plea, nothing the watching thousands can carry away as weakness. The chroniclers who record the number are hostile witnesses as often as friendly ones, which is itself remembered afterward as its own kind of testimony: even those who came to see a heretic punished cannot make him flinch in the way punishment is supposed to make a man flinch.
suggested_refs: The riverbank execution ground near Bab Khurasan, Baghdad

stops.name: Baghdad, the hands and feet cut off
stops.campa: After the scourging the executioner severs his hands and then his feet, the standard punishment of the age for those condemned as corrupters of the realm. Al-Husayn is said to smile at the sight of his own blood on the ground, and to smear his stumped face with what remains of it, so that he should not go pale before the crowd like a man drained by fear, but stand marked red like a man dressed for a wedding rather than a man carried to a scaffold, to the last insisting that this hour is a joy appointed rather than a horror endured.
stops.quote: Much blood has gone out of me. I realize that my face will have grown pale... I rubbed blood over my face so that I might appear rose-cheeked in your eyes. The cosmetic of heroes is their blood.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on al-Hallaj, tr. A. J. Arberry
suggested_refs: The Morgan Library manuscript miniature, 'Execution of Husain ibn Mansur al-Hallaj'

stops.name: Baghdad, raised on the gibbet, the stones and the rose of Shibli
stops.campa: Hoisted onto the gibbet before the whole crowd, al-Husayn is pelted with stones by spectators who have come to see a blasphemer punished. Among them stands Abu Bakr al-Shibli, once his companion in the path, who to conform throws something too: a clod of earth in Attar's telling, a single rose in the tellings that come after. At that touch, and not at the volley of stone, al-Husayn sighs aloud. Asked why so light a thing should wound where rock could not, he answers that the stone-throwers do not know what they do and have their excuse, but Shibli knows.
stops.quote: Because those who cast stones do not know what they are doing. They have an excuse. From him it comes hard to me, for he knows that he ought not to fling at me.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on al-Hallaj, tr. A. J. Arberry (Muslim Saints and Mystics)
suggested_refs: The clod of Shibli in Attar; the rose of Shibli in the later Persian and Sufi art of the martyrdom

stops.name: Baghdad, the final words and the beheading
stops.campa: As the sentence reaches its end, al-Husayn cries out once more over the crowd, words his own servant Ibrahim ibn Fatik will carry away and repeat for the rest of his life: that all that matters to the one lost in ecstasy is that the Unique should reduce him to Unity. He then recites, in the same breath, the verse of the Qur'an on those who hasten toward the Hour and those who wait for it in reverent fear, knowing it to be the truth. On these words the sword falls, and the head of al-Hallaj is struck from his body before the assembled thousands.
stops.quote: All that matters for the ecstatic is that the Unique should reduce him to Unity.
stops.quote_source: Last words transmitted through Ibrahim ibn Fatik in the Akhbar al-Hallaj, in Massignon's rendering of 'hasb al-wajid ifrad al-wahid lahu'; Attar gives the same saying as 'Love of the One is isolation of the One'
suggested_refs: Qur'an 42:18, the verse recited with his last breath, as recorded by eyewitnesses

stops.name: Baghdad, the body burned
stops.campa: On the day after the killing, as al-Husayn had told the stranger who asked him what love is that love itself would be shown him day by day, the trunk of his body is doused in oil on the same riverbank and set alight before another crowd, the fire kept burning until nothing recognizable as a man remains on the ground where the gibbet had stood only a day before. The head, already carried off separately, is spared the flame and given a different fate, one that will carry his name farther than his living body ever walked.
suggested_refs: The site of the burning, on the Tigris bank near Bab Khurasan

stops.name: Baghdad, the ashes on the Tigris and the head sent to Khorasan
stops.campa: On the third day the ashes of the burned body are gathered and cast into the Tigris from the height of a minaret, so that the river itself carries away what fire has left of him. His head, meanwhile, is left exposed on the great bridge of Baghdad for two days before being sent east to Khorasan, where it is paraded from province to province as proof to the frontier towns he once preached in that the man who cried Ana'l-Haqq is dead. A cenotaph rises at the execution ground and draws pilgrims for nearly a thousand years, until a Tigris flood in the 1920s sweeps it from the bank.
suggested_refs: The cenotaph of al-Hallaj on the Tigris bank, a pilgrimage site until its loss in a 1920s flood
Farid al-Din Attar, Mantiq al-Tayr (The Conference of the Birds), where al-Hallaj becomes the climactic exemplar of self-annihilation in God

stops.name: Baghdad, the ashes will not be quiet and the robe on the bank
stops.campa: The ashes will not be quiet. Floating on the surface they go on crying the same two words the man cried in the mosque of al-Mansur, and the Tigris begins to rise, until Baghdad stands in danger of drowning under its own river. His servant remembers what the master had said: lay my robe before the water. He carries the robe down and spreads it on the bank. The waters fall back, the ashes fall silent, and what is left of them is gathered up and buried. The city is spared by the cloak of the man it has just burned.
stops.quote: When they cast my ashes into the Tigris, Baghdad will be in peril of drowning under the water. Lay my robe in front of the water, or Baghdad will be destroyed.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, chapter on al-Hallaj, tr. A. J. Arberry
suggested_refs: The flooding Tigris stilled by al-Hallaj's robe, the closing miracle of Attar's account
